summary: Describes extensions to OSPF version 2 for intra-area traffic engineering, carried in Opaque Link State Advertisements. They let routers advertise extra link information that supports choosing paths based on more than simple shortest distance. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Maps usually show just distance. This adds notes like how wide each road is, so traffic planners can choose paths that avoid jams instead of always taking the shortest way.

questions: what is a traffic engineering lsa
what are ospf opaque lsa type 10
what sub tlvs does the ospf link tlv have
subtitle: How OSPF routers advertise bandwidth, colors and other link attributes so paths can be chosen by more than distance.

tldr.problem: Plain OSPF advertises only enough about each link to compute shortest paths. Traffic engineering needs more, such as how much bandwidth is free on a link and which administrative groups it belongs to.
tldr.mechanism: Routers flood a new Traffic Engineering LSA, carried as a type 10 (area-local) Opaque LSA. It holds nested TLVs: a Router Address TLV and a Link TLV with sub-TLVs for link type, bandwidth, metric and administrative group.
tldr.outcome: Each router can build a traffic engineering database for its area and compute constrained paths without changing normal OSPF routing. The RFC is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 4203 and RFC 5786.

today: RFC 3630 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2370 and is itself updated by RFC 4203 and RFC 5786. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Extending OSPF for Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
RFC 3630 adds traffic engineering (TE) capabilities to OSPF Version 2 (RFC 2328). The extensions describe a traffic engineering topology, including bandwidth and administrative constraints, and distribute it within one OSPF area. The semantic content is essentially identical to the corresponding IS-IS extensions, and the authors expect the OSPF extensions to keep mirroring them.

The RFC says that a more accurate name for the work is extended link attributes: it simply adds more attributes to links in OSPF advertisements. A router can use the resulting traffic engineering database to monitor link attributes, to compute paths locally under constraints (for example, only links of a given color with at least 10Mbps unreserved), or to support global traffic engineering from a traffic matrix.

The scope is deliberately narrow. Only intra-area distribution is covered. Reservation state is captured for point-to-point links, but may not be accurate for multi-access links with more than two devices, and unnumbered links are not supported. Flooding is unchanged: routers that do not understand TE LSAs MUST flood them like any other type 10 Opaque LSA.
sections.eli5: Routers already share a simple map. This document lets them also share extra notes about each road, but only inside one neighborhood, and only for certain kinds of roads.

sections.title: The Traffic Engineering LSA
sections.content:
The extension uses the Opaque LSA of RFC 2370. Only type 10 Opaque LSAs are used, which have area flooding scope. One new LSA is defined, the Traffic Engineering LSA. It describes routers, point-to-point links and connections to multi-access networks. The existing Network LSA is considered sufficient for describing multi-access links.

The LSA ID has eight bits of type data and 24 bits of type-specific data. The TE LSA uses type 1, and the remaining 24 bits are an Instance field that lets one system source several TE LSAs, up to 16777216 of them. The LSA ID has no topological significance.

After the standard LSA header, the payload is made of nested TLVs (type, length, value). The length counts only the value in octets. Each TLV is padded to four-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in the length, so a three-octet value has a total TLV size of eight octets. Nested TLVs are also 32-bit aligned, and unrecognized types are ignored.

An LSA contains one top-level TLV. Two are defined: type 1, Router Address, and type 2, Link.
sections.eli5: The notes travel in a standard envelope. Inside, each note has a label, a size and the message, and everything is padded to fit neat boxes. If a router does not know a label, it just skips that note.

sections.title: Router Address and Link Attributes
sections.content:
The Router Address TLV (type 1, length 4) carries a stable IP address of the advertising router that is reachable whenever there is any connectivity to it, typically a loopback address. It must appear in exactly one TE LSA originated by a router. If the router uses its BGP router ID as the BGP next hop, the Router Address SHOULD be the same. When IS-IS TE is also running, the address lets a router recognize that an IS-IS node and an OSPF node are the same device.

The Link TLV (type 2) describes a single link and is built from sub-TLVs in any order. Only one Link TLV is carried per LSA, so topology changes can be advertised at fine granularity. Link Type and Link ID are mandatory and appear exactly once; the others appear at most once.

  • Link Type: 1 point-to-point or 2 multi-access.
  • Link ID: the neighbor's Router ID for point-to-point links, or the designated router's interface address for multi-access links.
  • Local and Remote Interface IP Address: used to tell parallel links apart. For multi-access links the remote address is 0.0.0.0, or the sub-TLV may be omitted.
  • Traffic Engineering Metric: an administrator-assigned metric that may differ from the normal OSPF metric.
  • Maximum Bandwidth: the true link capacity in this direction, in bytes per second.
  • Maximum Reservable Bandwidth: what may be reserved, which may exceed the maximum bandwidth (oversubscription). It SHOULD be user-configurable and defaults to the Maximum Bandwidth.
  • Unreserved Bandwidth: eight values, one for each setup priority 0 through 7, initially all equal to the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth.
  • Administrative Group: a 32-bit mask in which each set bit is a group the link belongs to, also called Resource Class/Color.

Bandwidth values use the 32-bit IEEE floating point format.
sections.eli5: For each road the router writes down what kind of road it is, who is at the other end, how many lanes it really has, how many may be booked, how many are still free for each kind of customer, and what color tag it has.

sections.title: When Routers Originate and Use TE LSAs
sections.content:
Routers originate TE LSAs whenever the contents change and whenever OSPF otherwise requires it, such as an LSA refresh. Not every change has to be flooded at once. An implementation MAY set thresholds, for example a bandwidth change threshold, that trigger immediate flooding, and send other changes after a short interval. Origination SHOULD be rate-limited to at most one TE LSA every MinLSInterval.

When a router receives a changed TE LSA or Network LSA, it should update its traffic engineering database. No Shortest Path First or other route calculation is needed.
sections.eli5: When something changes, a router sends an update, but it does not shout every tiny change right away. The listeners just update their notes without redoing the whole map.

sections.title: Compatibility with Routers That Lack TE
sections.content: There should be no interoperability issues with routers that do not implement these extensions, because they silently ignore the Opaque LSAs. The cost is that the traffic engineering topology will be missing pieces. If the topology is still connected, TE paths can still be calculated and ought to work.
sections.eli5: Routers that do not know the new notes just pass them along without reading them. The map has a few blank spots, but you can usually still find a route.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Opaque LSAs are not used for SPF computation or normal routing, so these extensions have no effect on IP routing itself. Tampering with TE LSAs could however affect traffic engineering computations. The RFC suggests applying any mechanism used to secure normal OSPF LSA transmission equally to all Opaque LSAs, including TE LSAs, and notes that the mechanisms in RFC 2328 and RFC 2154 apply to Opaque LSAs. It also suggests that any future OSPFv2 authentication mechanism be general enough to cover Opaque LSAs.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaking in fake notes would not break the normal map, but could trick planners into picking bad roads. So the notes should be protected the same way as the main map.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: Top-level TE LSA types and sub-TLV types have been registered with IANA. For top-level types, 3-32767 are assigned by Standards Action, 32768-32777 are for experimental use and MUST NOT be mentioned by RFCs, and 32778-65535 are not to be assigned until a Standards Track RFC covers the range. Sub-TLV types follow the same pattern, except that Standards Action covers 10-32767.
sections.eli5: There is a list of label numbers. Some are handed out carefully, some are free to play with, and some are kept in reserve for later.
